issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of an expenditure as revenue or capital depends on the size of the amount or whether it was paid in a lump sum or by instalments.

law.fact_text: The key test to determine if an expenditure is capital or revenue is the purpose, aim, and object for which the payment was made.
law.law_text: If the expenditure is made for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is a capital expenditure. If it is made for running the business or working it with a view to produce profits, it is a revenue expenditure.

law.fact_text: The size of the payment (large or small) and the manner of payment (lump sum or instalments) are not the deciding factors.
law.law_text: The answer to the question whether the money paid was a revenue expenditure or capital expenditure does not depend upon whether the amount paid is large or small or whether it was paid in a lumpsum or by instalments.

application.fact_text: The Court applied this principle by stating that if the object of a payment is to acquire a capital asset, the payment is capital in nature, even if it is made in instalments over time.
application.law_text: If the object of making the payment is to acquire a capital asset the payment would partake of the character of a capital payment even though it is not made in a lumpsum but by instalments over a period of time.

application.fact_text: Conversely, the Court noted that a payment made for the purpose of carrying on business is a revenue expenditure, even if the amount is large.
application.law_text: On the contrary, payment made in the course of and for the purpose of carrying on business or trading activity would be revenue expenditure even though the payment is of a large amount...

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that the size of an expenditure or its payment method (lump sum vs. instalments) determines its character. The Court held that the decisive factor is the purpose of the payment. If the purpose is to acquire an asset for the enduring benefit of the business, it is a capital expenditure, regardless of the amount or how it is paid. If the purpose is to run the day-to-day operations of the business, it is a revenue expenditure.

issue.issue_text: Whether an expenditure is considered a capital expenditure if its purpose is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, irrespective of the source of payment or whether it was paid periodically.

facts: The appellant was appointed as the sole selling agent for a corporation.
As consideration for this appointment, the appellant agreed to pay a pre-existing debt owed by the previous agent to the corporation.
This payment was made not as a lump sum, but in installments through deductions from the sales commission due to the appellant.
law: The primary test to distinguish between a capital and a revenue expenditure is the 'aim and object' or 'purpose' of the payment.
If the expenditure is made to acquire or bring into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, it is a capital expenditure.
Conversely, if an expenditure is made for running the business or working it to produce profits, it is a revenue expenditure.

The Court held that factors such as the source of the payment (capital or income), the size of the amount, or the manner of payment (lump sum or periodic installments) are immaterial and of 'no consequence' in determining the expenditure's fundamental character.
application: The Court identified the 'sole selling agency right' acquired by the appellant as a capital asset that provided an 'enduring benefit' to the business.
The payments made by the appellant were the consideration for acquiring this capital asset.
The Court reasoned that this was a liability undertaken for the purpose of acquiring the asset, not a liability incurred in the course of running the business.
Therefore, the fact that the payment was made periodically through deductions from commission, rather than as a single lump sum, did not alter its essential nature as a capital expenditure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an expenditure is a capital expenditure if its purpose is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business. The source of the payment or the manner in which it is paid (lump sum or periodically) does not change the character of the expenditure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of an expenditure as revenue or capital depends on the size of the amount or whether it was paid in a lump sum or by instalments.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the method of payment mattered. By contending that they could make no claim to the amount retained by the corporation, they suggested that payment via periodic deductions from commission should be treated differently from a lump sum payment, and thus not as a capital expenditure.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, upheld by the court, was that the fact the amount was paid in instalments through deductions, rather than in a lump sum, does not make any difference to its classification as a capital expenditure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an expenditure is considered a capital expenditure if its purpose is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, irrespective of the source of payment or whether it was paid periodically.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the payment was an application of their income (commission) to discharge a liability, and focused on the mechanism of payment (periodic deductions) to imply it was a revenue expense, thereby arguing against the primacy of the 'purpose' test in this context.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument, adopted by the court, was that the payment was made for the purpose of acquiring a sole selling agency right, which is a capital asset providing an enduring benefit. This purpose definitively makes the expenditure capital in nature, regardless of the fact it was paid periodically through deductions from commission.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The determination of whether an expenditure is capital or revenue depends on the purpose for which the payment was made. If the object of the payment is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, the expenditure is capital in nature. The amount of the payment, the manner of payment (lump sum or installments), and the source of the funds are not determinative of the expenditure's character.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The determination of whether an expenditure is for revenue or capital does not depend on the size of the amount, or whether it was paid in a lump sum or by instalments. The classification depends entirely on the purpose for which the payment was made. If the object of the payment is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, the expenditure is capital in nature, regardless of the source of the payment or the periodicity of the payments.
legal_tests_applied: The 'Purpose Test' for expenditure: The court examines the aim and object of the expenditure. If the purpose is to acquire a capital asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of the business, the expenditure is capital. Conversely, if the payment is made in the course of and for the purpose of carrying on the business or trading activity, it is a revenue expenditure.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that it could make no claim to the amount retained by the corporation was deemed to make 'no material difference so far as the true nature of that amount was concerned.'

The court characterized the payment not as an expense incurred in the course of running the business, but as 'the application of income to discharge a liability undertaken for the purpose of acquiring the sole selling agency right which was indisputably an asset of capital nature.'
The method of payment, through deductions from commission, was held to be irrelevant to the classification of the expenditure as capital.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the payment was made for a specific purpose: 'in consideration of being appointed the sole selling agent of the Kanpur Cotton Mills.'
The court determined that the sole selling agency right acquired by the appellant was 'indisputably an asset of capital nature.'
The respondent's position that the purpose of the expenditure dictates its character was upheld, making the method or periodicity of payment immaterial.
